newsitem.title: USA: Clinton releases medical data in response to Dole.
newsitem.headline: Clinton releases medical data in response to Dole.

text.p: Stung by complaints from Republican Bob Dole, the White House on Friday released President Bill Clinton's medical history to show that he had no major health problems.

Included in a packet of papers released was a report that he underwent a test for HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, in 1990 and it was negative. The test was described as part of an health insurance physical.

A four-page summary of Clinton's medical history by his physician, Dr. Connie Mariano, said Clinton has "no history of hypertension, diabetes, tuberculosis, sexually transmitted disease, cancer, stroke or heart disease."
The summary reported one problem that had not previously been disclosed -- that he suffers from high-frequency hearing loss. But it said his hearing for regular speech is normal.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the problem could be attributed to hearing gunshots at close range while hunting in Arkansas when he was growing up, or loud music from playing in his high school band.

Dole had repeatedly demanded that Clinton release his full medical records and suggested that his failure to do so meant the president may be hiding something. "Let's have your health records, Mr. President," Dole said on Thursday. "I gave them all of mine."

That led to a White House news briefing Thursday during a Clinton campaign trip in Fresno, California, where McCurry was asked bluntly whether the president had a sexually transmitted disease. McCurry said no and told reporters he was "astonished" the question had been raised.
The Dole campaign was still not satisfied and said Clinton's medical records should be reviewed by independent doctors such as New York Times specialist Dr. Lawrence Altman.

"The $64,000 question is, what didn't the White House release today? What was it that was so embarrassing that the White House felt the need to keep these records, if complete, from the American people?" said Dole's deputy campaign press secretary Christina Martin.
But McCurry said on Friday night the medical history was as "complete as it gets" and should lay questions about Clinton's health to rest "once and for all."
"If this don't do it, I can't imagine what else you'd need," he told reporters.

The report included supporting letters from Clinton's doctors. Absent, however, were the actual medical records as written by Clinton's doctors. McCurry said the were being withheld in the interest of "preserving the dignity of the office."
The White House also issued the medical history of Vice President Al Gore. It said Gore had a cancerous skin growth, common from sun exposure, surgically removed in 1993 with no recurrence.
Gore has mildly elevated cholesterol and high-frequency hearing loss. He smoked a pack a day of cigarettes from 1968 to 1973, but does not now smoke.

Clinton's report went over a lot of ground already covered in reports on Clinton's previous annual physicals: he suffers from seasonal allergies, voice hoarseness and has had several pre-cancerous skin eruptions resulting from skin exposure removed from his face. He also has stomach acid occasionally and lower back pain that resulted from a 1984 ski accident.
It said Clinton does not smoke cigarettes but "occasionally chews on cigars," drinks alcohol occasionally at social events, rarely uses caffeine and sleeps about six hours a night.
He had his tonsils removed in 1952, fractured his left leg in 1951 and had surgery on his sinuses in 1979 for sinusitis. An ingrown pimple on his neck was removed surgically earlier this month.

The report said his heart rate was a normal 55 beats per minute at his last physical last May and that a treadmill test showed his heart in good shape. His cholesterol is a normal 191, blood pressure a normal 126/70, and he weighed 216 pounds.
